# Expanding the PCET Thermochemistry of CpN3: N–H Bond Strengths of Metal-Free CpN3 Molecules and the Influence of Fe(CO)3 Coordination

**Authors:** David S. Tresp; Tim K. Schramm; Sanju Luhach; Amado Rosendo; Allison Houn; Tianyi Zhang; Amy Turtz; Jenny V. Lockard; Andreas Hansen; Demyan E. Prokopchuk

**Affiliations:** † Department of Chemistry, 67206Rutgers University-Newark, Newark, New Jersey 07102, United States | ‡ Mulliken Center for Theoretical Chemistry, Clausius Institute for Physical and Theoretical Chemistry, Rhenish Friedrich Wilhelms University of Bonn, Bonn 53115, Germany | § Department of Chemistry, 6740Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States

## Abstract

Amine rich cyclopentadienyl (CpN3) ligands are electronically distinct from classical Cp ligand architectures, as they exhibit fascinating proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) chemistry under acidic conditions in the presence and absence of transition metals. We now report that the exocyclic N–H bond of the isopropylamine moiety in [RCpN3]+ can be deprotonated under basic conditions (R = iPr, t Bu), enabling the experimental determination of N–H bond strengths via pK a and redox potential measurements in acetonitrile. From these data, the experimentally determined N–H acidity and bond dissociation free energy of [iPrCpN3]+ are pK a = 22.6 and BDFE = 82.6 kcal/mol in acetonitrile. These results are linked with the known C–H bond thermochemistry data of [iPrCpN3]+, and computational (DFT) data sets are in excellent agreement with experiment. The exocyclic N–H bond acidity was also investigated with [iPrCpN3]+ coordinated to Fe­(CO)3, and surprisingly, its pK a is largely unperturbed in the presence of a transition metal (pK a = 20–24 (experiment); 23.7 (DFT)). This prompted us to investigate the formal oxidation state of the iron center in our “FeII” starting material, with 57Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy, XANES spectroscopy, charge distribution via reporter (CDVR) analysis, and computations, revealing that the metal center is best interpreted as having a +2 formal oxidation state. These data suggest that the electronic perturbations at the electron-rich CpN3 ligand upon coordination to FeII do not significantly influence the exocyclic N–H bond acidity.

## Introduction

Lauded for their tunability and robustness, cyclopentadienyl (Cp) ligands have been used extensively in homogeneous catalysis to stabilize Earth-abundant transition metals. − While Cp ligands are largely thought to act as chemically innocent spectators, several reports have found Cp to be chemically noninnocent, enabling the ring to act as a reservoir for proton (H+), hydrogen atom (H•), and/or hydride (H–) transfer. − In this context, our group has been particularly interested in the chemically noninnocent behavior of electron rich triamine-substituted cyclopentadienyl molecules (CpN3; Figure ). We first discovered that the piano–stool complexes [(iPrCpN3)­Fe­(CO)2(NCMe)]+ act as H2 production electrocatalysts under acidic conditions, where endo-protonation of a carbon atom in the Cp ring is mechanistically essential in the presence of exogenous acid (Figure A). This catalyst was first synthetically accessed by Renaud and co-workers through the formal oxidation of a Fe0 precursor, such as Fe2(CO)9 by “cyclopentadienylium” precursor ([CpN3]+) salts, generating a series of [(RCpN3)­FeII(CO)3]+ complexes which can be viewed as protonated amine variants of Knölker-type catalysts. ,− Renaud and co-workers have explored a variety of these Fe catalysts with nitrogen and oxygen donors appended to the cyclopentadienyl ring, finding them competent at catalyzing reductive amination, − hydrazine alkylation, CO2 reduction, and imine hydrogenation. Analogous to Knölker-type systems, these catalysts act as tandem hydrogen transfer agents, taking an H2 equivalent from alcohols and delivering it to substrates. Moreover, site-selective hydride transfer to the CpN3 ring is also feasible in the presence of exogenous H– transfer agents (NaBH4, LiAlH4, NaHBEt3). The mechanism of hydride addition is strongly dependent on the identity of the hydride donor, with the complex shown in Figure B forming via reduction of Renaud’s complex, [(iPrCpN3)­Fe­(CO)3]+, in the presence of NaHBEt3 and CO(g). In a recent example, Cp ring activation has been proposed as a plausible pathway in the dehydrogenative coupling of phosphines catalyzed by a Cp*CoI2CO complex.

In contrast, the reactivity of classical Cp ring derivatives with H+, H•, and H– in the absence of transition metals has been explored to a far lesser extent. Perhaps the only reliable metal-free Cp thermochemical measurements are for 1,3-cyclopentadiene (C5H6), with pK a = 18.0 and homolytic bond dissociation free energy (BDFE) of 74.7 in DMSO. , Recently, we found that the CpN3 platform exhibits facile proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) thermochemistry without metal complexation (Figure C), showing “iminium-like” π electron delocalization over the three exocyclic C–N bonds. The cyclopentadiene-iminium cation [ iPr Cp N3 ] + can be selectively protonated at an endocyclic carbon center to generate [ iPr Cp N3 H] 2+ the same position that is protonated during electrocatalytic H2 production. ,, Furthermore, we established that 1e– reduction of [ iPr Cp N3 H] 2+ to [ iPr Cp N3 H] •+ results in an incredibly weak homolytic C–H bond dissociation free energy (BDFE) of 51.8 kcal/mol in acetonitrile, which is calculated using the Bordwell equation. − This value is substantially weaker than the C–H BDFEs of other organic molecules such as triphenylmethane (BDFECH = 75.7 kcal/mol, DMSO) , and 1,4-cyclohexadiene (BDFECH = 67.8 kcal/mol, gas phase).

In the process of exploring alternative synthetic routes to make new transition metal complexes using [ iPr Cp N3 ] + , we serendipitously discovered that the exocyclic N–H bond of [ iPr Cp N3 ] + is susceptible to deprotonation under basic conditions in the absence of transition metals (Figure ; pink H atom), resembling well-studied cyclopentadienones. − Thus, we now report the N–H bond thermochemistry of [ iPr Cp N3 ] + and the derivative [ tBu Cp N3 ] + , expanding our thermochemical understanding of the multisite PCET thermochemistry with this family of molecules. Gratifyingly, the experimental data are in excellent agreement with our DFT computations, which employ an efficient multilevel workflow validated through comprehensive method benchmarking. Furthermore, we performed N–H pK a measurements on [( iPr Cp N3 )­Fe­(CO) 3 ] and compared its pK a data with metal-free [ iPr Cp N3 ] + . Additional insights into the iron’s formal oxidation state before ligand deprotonation were also acquired using IR, Mössbauer, and XANES spectroscopies in combination with computational (DFT) and charge distribution via reporter (CDVR) analysis.

## Results and Discussion

The known cyclopentadiene-iminium salt [ iPr Cp N3 ]­[BF 4 ] (iPrCpN3 = 6-isopropyl-1,4-dimethyl-5,7-diphenyl-2,3,4,6-tetrahydrocyclopenta­[b]­pyrazin-6-ylium) and new tert-butyl analogue [ tBu Cp N3 ]­[BF 4 ] (tBuCpN3 = 6-tert-butyl-1,4-dimethyl-5,7-diphenyl-2,3,4,6-tetrahydrocyclopenta­[b]­pyrazin-6-ylium) were prepared by reacting the ketone precursor with triethyloxonium tetrafluoroborate and amine (Figure , top). In the presence of KOtBu in THF, deprotonation of the N–H moiety smoothly occurs to generate the neutral cyclopentadienimines R Cp′ N3 (R = iPr, t Bu) in 63% and 29% yield, respectively (Figure , top). 1H NMR spectra of R Cp′ N3 in C6D6 show that most resonances become more shielded due to a decrease in overall charge, and the tertiary alkyl hydrogen within the iPr moiety of iPr Cp′ N3 collapses from a complex multiplet into a simple septet (δ = 4.03 ppm, 3 J HH = 7.0 Hz).

The metrical parameters obtained via single crystal X-ray diffraction for R Cp′ N3 and [ R Cp N3 ] + are summarized in Table , and several notable features are common to both iPr and t Bu derivatives. First, the exocyclic “iminium” C–N bond (Entry 6) and two delocalized “alkene” C–C bonds (Entries 2, 4) all contract upon deprotonation, indicating their increase in multiple bond character. The exoyclic C–N bonds shorten by 0.03–0.04 Å after deprotonation while the adjacent C–C bonds of R Cp′ N3 (Entries 1, 5) lengthen by 0.03–0.05 Å, indicating their transition to single-bond character. All of the measured changes in bond metrics can also be qualitatively observed in the corresponding solution phase structures as calculated by density functional theory.

Due to the facile deprotonation of the N–H moieties to produce R Cp′ N3 with strong base, we were motivated to probe the N–H bond strength of [ iPr Cp N3 ] + in acetonitrile by surveying its reactivity of [ iPr Cp N3 ] + with bases of varying strength to determine pK a(N–H). [ iPr Cp N3 ] + can be fully deprotonated with 1,8-Diazabicyclo[5.4.0]­undec-7-ene (DBU, pK a MeCN = 24.31), but pyrollidine is not strong enough to deprotonate it (pK a MeCN = 19.62). With this pK a bracketing data in hand, choosing a base of intermediate strength such as (+)-sparteine (pK a MeCN = 21.67) results in partial deprotonation at room temperature. However, the exchange process between the acid–base pair at 25 °C severely broadens the N–H signals at 9.83 and 6.54 ppm in the 1H NMR spectrum in CD3CN, making integrations unreliable and hampering our efforts to accurately measure the N–H acidity (Figure ). Moreover, using other 1H NMR resonances for quantification proved challenging due to significant peak overlap between the acid and conjugate base. An NMR sample containing an equilibrium mixture of [ iPr Cp′ N3 ] + , (+)-sparteine, and their respective acid/base conjugates in CD3CN was cooled to −40 °C, allowing us to clearly observe the acid–base pair and integrate of the N–H resonances of [ iPr Cp′ N3 ] + and conjugate acid of (+)-sparteine. An equilibrium constant (K eq) could be calculated below room temperature, and raising the temperature in 10 °C increments enabled us to collect enough data points to conduct Van’t Hoff analysis and extrapolate the equilibrium constant under standard-state conditions (Figure , inset). Thus, pK a MeCN = 22.6 ± 0.1 for the N–H bond of [ iPr Cp N3 ]­[BF 4 ]. In the case of the [ tBu Cp N3 ]­[BF 4 ] upon deprotonation, nearly all 1H resonances broaden (Figure S9), which we propose results from greater steric hindrance around the amine, restricting full phenyl ring rotation, with additional rigidification occurring upon deprotonation due to increased C–N π-bond character. This increased broadening made K eq and subsequent pK a determination by NMR unreliable.

To expand on the redox chemistry of the CpN3 molecules, [ iPr Cp N3 ]­[BF 4 ], iPr Cp′ N3 , [ tBu Cp N3 ]­[BF 4 ] and tBu Cp′ N3 were all electrochemically characterized by cyclic voltammetry (CV) in acetonitrile and referenced versus ferrocenium/ferrocene (Fc+/0). In all four cases, CVs were run in the anodic direction (Figure ). A commonly used electrolyte such as [ n Bu4N]­[PF6] often resulted in irreversible or quasi-reversible redox features at all studied scan rates for these molecules, therefore we opted to use the more inert electrolyte [Bu4N]­[B­(C6F5)4] for all compounds in this study. First, we found that [ iPr Cp N3 ]­[BF 4 ] has a reversible 1e– redox couple wave at all tested scan rates (E 1/2([ iPr Cp N3 ] + ) = 0.52 V; Figure a). Upon deprotonation, the redox potential of deprotonated iPr Cp′ N3 becomes more cathodic (E 1/2( iPr Cp′ N3 ) = −0.04 V), generating the cation radical [ iPr Cp N3 ] +• and becoming partially reversible at scan rates below 15 V/s (Figure b). The redox potential of [ tBu Cp N3 ]­[BF 4 ] is nearly identical to that of [ iPr Cp N3 ]­[BF 4 ], however, its redox potential is pseudoreversible below 0.5 V/s (Figure c). Finally, the redox potential for tBu Cp′ N3 is slightly more cathodic than iPr Cp′ N3 owing to the increased donor character of the t Bu moiety (E 1/2 = 0.02 V; Figure d).

The newly acquired electrochemical and pK a data enable us to expand the C–H and N–H PCET thermochemistry data sets for the iPrCpN3 molecules. Building on our earlier report that contains C–H bond thermochemistry for [ iPr Cp N3 ] + as shown in Scheme , protonation generates [ iPr Cp N3 H] 2+ which has a BDFECH = 81.0 kcal/mol, a value about 30 kcal/mol higher than that of the radical monocation (BDFECH([ iPr Cp N3 H] •+ ) = 52 kcal/mol). Thus, reacting [ iPr Cp N3 ] + with a suitable strong oxidant is expected to generate a potent H-atom acceptor. The aminium salt and oxidant dubbed “Magic Blue”, [(p-C6H5Br)3N]•+, has a redox potential of E 1/2 = 0.67 V in MeCN, and the [B­(C6F5)4]− salt was prepared in 88% yield using a modified synthetic procedure. Its molecular structure was further confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction (Figure S16). Reacting [ iPr Cp N3 ] + with [(p-C6H5Br)3N]­[B­(C6F5)4] in MeCN at −44 °C resulted in a color change from deep blue to deep green, which upon warming resulted in a yellow solution. Analysis by 1H NMR revealed that the dication [ iPr Cp N3 H] 2+ was generated in 66% yield, which is proposed to be the result of facile H-atom transfer to the dication radical generated in situ, either from the parent compound, solvent, or a combination of both. Combining the redox potential data of the deprotonated iPr Cp′ N3 with the experimentally determined pK a data allows us to extract a homolytic N–H BDFE of 82.6 kcal/mol (Scheme ). This is very similar to the homolytic BDFEs of other secondary alkylamines in MeCN, such as Et2NH (BDFEMeCN = 82.2 kcal/mol) or nBu2NH (BDFEMeCN = 82.5 kcal/mol). Moreover, it is similar to the effective BDFE of Magic Blue (BDFEeff, MeCN, pyridine = 85.2 kcal/mol). In this context, we also emphasize the striking agreement of the acquired experimental data with our computed thermochemical results, resulting from an efficient multilevel workflow (see Scheme , and the Computational Methods in the Appendix and Supporting Information for details). The PCET thermochemical data for tBu Cp′ N3 are very similar and provided in the Supporting Information (Figure S17).

*1: PCET Thermochemistry in MeCN for C–H32 and N–H Bonds Housed within iPr Cp′ N3*

To arrive at such accurate computational thermochemical data, we leveraged an efficient multilevel workflow, which allows for extensive conformational exploration of all molecules at lower levels of theories while still maintaining high accuracy for the final values in computed redox potentials, BDFEs, etc. For this, we employed the fast semiempirical quantum mechanical method GFN1-xTB within CREST and ORCA (GOAT approach), followed by conformational energetic reranking with the robust r2SCAN-3c composite method in CENSO, which was also used to relax the structures to their final geometries. Subsequently, the resulting lowest-energy conformer was used to evaluate a total of 90 combinations of density functional approximations and implicit solvation models (15 functionals, 6 solvation models), while also considering the influence of orbital instabilities on the results via spin-projection techniques. , Finally, this comprehensive method benchmark yielded the PWPB95-D4 − functional combined with the large def2-QZVPP , basis set and CPCM , -DRACO implicit solvation as our most accurate level of theory, when proper spin projection is applied. Please refer to the Supporting Information for more details on our calculations and the complete redox potential benchmark data with a discussion thereof.

To compare the N–H bond strength of the ligand when complexed to Fe, we explored the deprotonation chemistry [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ], a known precursor for H2 production electrocatalysis under acidic conditions. , When deprotonated with tBuOK in THF, MeCN, or Toluene, the thermodynamic product is the poorly soluble dimeric Fe­(I) species [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 2 ] 2 , which has been previously characterized (Scheme ). We propose that initial deprotonation occurs to generate a transient Fe0 complex iPr Cp′ N3 Fe­(CO) 3 in situ, with subsequent H atom abstraction and CO dissociation. The reaction outcome is similar in less coordinating solvents such as THF and toluene, suggesting that MeCN coordination is not required to facilitate dimerization. These unfortunate follow–up reactions make pK a determination via equilibrium analysis challenging. However, we can bracket the N–H pK a by surveying the reactivity of [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] with different bases. For instance, DBU fully deprotonates [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ], followed by the expected dimerization (Figure S12), whereas pyrrolidine is unable to deprotonate the complex, therefore bracketing the N–H pK a between 19.6 to 24.3 in MeCN (Figure S13). The DFT calculations enable us to refine this measurement with a pK a(N–H) estimate of 23.7 in MeCN, placing the pK a(N–H) of [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] more toward the upper end of the experimentally determined pK a range, even when considering an error of up to ±2 pK a units. To our surprise, this indicates that coordinating [ iPr Cp N3 ] + to Fe induces little to no change in the N–H acidity, suggesting that significant electronic perturbations to the Cp ring do not alter the electronic nature of the N–H bond. We did not explore this deprotonation chemistry in the presence of more weakly coordinating anions (i.e., B­(ArF)4 –, B­(C6F5)4 –), therefore we cannot conclusively rule out the participation of PF6 – during dimerization.

*2: Reactivity of [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] under Basic Conditions*

The existence of the transient Fe0 complex iPr Cp′ N3 Fe­(CO) 3 is supported by immediately acquiring 1H after adding DBU to an NMR tube containing [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] dissolved in CD3CN. The 1H resonance for the N–H moiety (3.96 ppm, d, 3 J HH = 9.6 Hz) fully disappears, and the isopropyl C–H resonance (2.81 ppm, doublet of septets, 3 J HH = 9.5, 6.5 Hz) collapses into a simple septet (2.86 ppm, 3 J HH = 6.3 Hz) and becomes more shielded (Figure S12). Initially, upon deprotonation with DBU, the solution slightly lightens from deep yellow to pale yellow, before further reacting to a deep green solution that slowly yields [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 2 ] 2 as X-ray quality crystals.

To gain further insights into the electronic changes upon deprotonation, we performed an in situ deprotonation followed by IR spectroscopic analysis. The CO stretching frequencies of the parent [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] are 2042, 1992, and 1965 cm–1, representing a vastly more electron-rich iron center compared to the CO stretching frequencies of [Cp*Fe­(CO)3]+ (2135 and 2072 cm–1) or [CpFe­(CO)3]+ (2120 and 2068 cm–1). − Upon deprotonation with DBU, the IR spectrum reveals broad but intense CO stretching frequencies centered at 2024, 1960, and 1940 cm–1 and a CN stretch at 1646 cm–1 (Figure S14), which are tentatively assigned to the neutral iPr Cp′ N3 Fe­(CO) 3 . The stretching frequencies of iPr Cp′ N3 Fe­(CO) 3 are in fact nearly identical to a structurally analogous Fe0 cylopentadienone complex presented by Renaud et al., which exhibits CO stretches at 2027, 1962, and 1947 cm–1. The DFT-computed IR spectrum for iPr Cp′ N3 Fe­(CO) 3 does not conclusively rule out this assignment given that the observed deviations still lie within reasonable error ranges (cf., observed deviation for the dimer). However, even assuming a correct assignment, these stretching frequencies are puzzling as they are not significantly shifted with respect to the starting material, which therefore casts some doubt on the formal oxidation state assignment of [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ]. Consequently, we wondered if the resonance structure shown on the left of Scheme would be a more suitable representation.

First, we examined the electronic structure of [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] using zero-field 57Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy. The complex exhibited an isomer shift of 0.13 mm/s and quadrupole splitting of 1.70 mm/s (Figure , left). This is very similar to an isoelectronic Fe­(II) compound, [Cp*Fe­(CO)3]­[PF6], exhibiting an isomer shift of 0.08 mm/s and quadrupole splitting of 1.85 mm/s. The slightly higher isomer shift of [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] (0.12 mm/s versus 0.08 mm/s for the parent Cp* compound) is consistent with an overall more electron-donating CpN3 ligand than the Cp* ligand. Strong π-donicity into the Fe 3d orbitals results in a higher electron density in the 3d orbitals and a greater degree of shielding of core 1s/2s electrons. This reduction in the 1s/2s electron density at the Fe nucleus thus leads to a more positive isomer shift. This does not clearly indicate a shift away from a formal FeII to Fe0 oxidation state; however, it also does not conclusively rule it out.

To further probe the electronic structure, a sample of [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] was analyzed via XAS and compared with reference complex [Cp*Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ]. Figure (right) displays an overlay of the XANES spectra for [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] compared to [Cp*Fe­(CO)3]­[PF6] and Fe-foil references (associated derivative spectra shown in Figure S20). The XANES spectra for each complex show distinct pre-edge features corresponding to 1s to 3d transitions in both cases. The similar lower edge energy of [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] compared to the classical FeII reference complex [Cp*Fe­(CO)3]­[PF6] is consistent with a +2 formal oxidation state assignment for [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ]. Complex [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] exhibits a pronounced high energy pre-edge peak at 7115.5 eV with a resolved lower-energy shoulder at 7112.8 eV, while [Cp*Fe­(CO)3]­[PF6] shows a main pre-edge peak at 7114.9 eV with lower energy shoulder at 7112.8 eV. These split pre-edge features observed in both complexes are consistent with literature precedent reported for acetylferrocene (FeII) and Fe­(COD)­(CO)3 (Fe0), illustrating how π-backbonding and reduced symmetry from the presence of Cp and diene ligands leads to a distorted coordination environment and orbital splitting. However, the edge shift to higher energy of the main pre-edge peak in [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] suggests a 3d-π* orbital interaction with a higher energy antibonding orbital housed within CpN3, possibly due to more stabilizing (i.e., more electron donating) CpN3 ligation.

With mounting evidence that Fe center likely adopts a formal oxidation state of +2, we also explored the electronic effects of the surrounding ligands using Wolczanski’s charge distribution via reporters (CDVR) method. , This method “flips” the oxidation state formalism by fixing the charge of Fe at +2.0 (c M), enabling extraction of the partial charge of bound CO (c CO) as a “reporter ligand” by using a molecule’s average IR stretching frequency (νCO, cm–1) and the empirical relationship c CO = (νCO – 2207)­cm–1/475 cm–1. Ultimately, this enables determination of the partial charge for the iPrCpN3 ligand (c CpN3). Following this, c CO for [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ]­[PF 6 ] is −0.44, which is very similar to the partial charges of CO for Fe­(CO)5 (c CO = −0.4). Combining this value with the overall charge of c ML = +1 for the iron complex [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ] + , the CDVR method suggests the partial charge for the iPrCpN3 ligand to be c CpN3 = +0.32, which bears a net positive charge (Figure ). This counterintuitive finding contrasts dramatically with the partial charge of the Cp* ligand for [Cp*Fe­(CO) 3 ] + (c Cp* = −0.35), suggesting that the iPrCpN3 ligand is an incredibly strong electron donor, yet still retains a partial (albeit diminished) positive charge upon coordination to Fe due to the delocalized iminium character of the C–N bonds throughout the ligand network. Based on the validated DFT protocols, computational work is currently ongoing to shed more light on the electronic structure of [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ] + .

## Conclusions

We have expanded our understanding of the multisite PCET thermochemistry for the amine-rich [ R Cp N3 ] + molecule under basic conditions, where deprotonation of the exocyclic amine yields neutral compounds amenable to equilibrium analysis via NMR spectroscopy and cyclic voltammetry (R = iPr, t Bu). In marked contrast to the C–H bond thermochemistry of the dicationic [ R Cp N3 H] 2+ , the N–H bond pK a of the monocationic [ R Cp N3 ] + species is approximately 10 pK a units higher, while the N–H BDFE increases by about 30 kcal/mol. Both these findings were nicely reproduced by our double-hybrid level DFT calculations, which generally yielded excellent agreement to all experimental thermochemical data after comprehensive functional benchmarking. We also explored the N–H acid–base chemistry upon coordinating [ iPr Cp N3 ] + to Fe­(CO)3, finding that upon deprotonation, the Fe complex irreversibly dimerizes through an unexplored mechanism which involves H atom transfer and CO loss. Strikingly, the N–H pK a is largely unaffected by the proximal metal center. This result prompted us to investigate the nature of the iron oxidation state in [ iPr Cp N3 Fe­(CO) 3 ] + using both Mössbauer and XANES spectroscopy. Collectively, these methods suggest that the iron center is in a +2 formal oxidation state, however the electron density at Fe appears to be modulated by a significant offloading of charge onto the three CO ligands from the strongly electron donating iPrCpN3 ligand. Further work is ongoing to understand how these redox-active CpN3 molecules, with or without transition metals, can be leveraged to facilitate catalytic reactions involving proton, electron, and/or hydrogen atom transfer.

### General Procedures

Compounds were handled under a nitrogen or argon atmosphere in a glovebox or via standard Schlenk techniques under nitrogen unless otherwise stated. Triethyloxonium tetrafluoroborate was handled in a glovebox, washed with diethyl ether, and dried under vacuum before use to remove acidic impurities, as these tended to decrease product yields and purities. [ iPr Cp N3 ]­[BF 4 ], 1,4-dimethyl-5,7-diphenyl-1,2,3,4-tetrahydro-6H-cyclopenta­[b]­pyrazin-6-one, [Cp*Fe­(CO)3]­[PF6], and [(p-C6H4Br)3N]­[B­(C6F5)4] (“Magic Blue BF20”) were prepared using known literature procedures. Workup of Magic Blue BF20 using the known procedure produced single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction, and the structure has been deposited to the CCDC (2451566). Commercially available reagents were used as received. Solvents were dried and degassed over alumina columns on a solvent purification system and stored overnight on 10% w/v molecular sieves before use. Celite was heated at 140 °C in a heating mantle for several hours, cooled under vacuum, and stored in a glovebox for use. Infrared spectra were recorded on a Thermo Nicolet FT-IR instrument. Elemental analyzes were performed by the CENTC Facility, Department of Chemistry, University of Rochester.

### NMR Spectroscopy

1H, 11B, 13C, and 19F NMR were collected on a Bruker Avance III 500 MHz NMR using either a 5 mm BBO broadband (31P-109Ag, 1H,19F) probe or 5 mm BBFO broadband (31P–15N plus 19F, 1H) Probe. NMR was referenced internally to residual 1H and 13C signals in the deuterated solvent. 11B and 19F NMR were referenced externally to BF3–OEt2 and CFCl3, respectively. For Van’t Hoff analyzes from the VT-NMR data, S/N (Signal to Noise) ratios were calculated for each signal in Topspin by using the “SINo” function. The relative error for peak integrals is 1/(S/N). For VT-NMR experiments, the probe temperature was calibrated using Sigma-Aldrich methanol-d 4 NMR reference standard.

### Mass Spectrometry

High-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) data were obtained by atmospheric pressure chemical ionization (APCI) in positive mode on an Orbitrap Exploris 240 instrument.

### X-ray Diffraction

Single crystals were mounted on a nylon loop and cooled to 100 K under a dry nitrogen stream before data collection unless otherwise stated. SCXRD was performed on a Rigaku XtaLAB Synergy-i diffractometer using CuKα with a HyPIX HPC detector. Structures were refined by full-matrix least-squares based on F2 with all reflections (SHELXTL V5.10; G. Sheldrick, Siemens XRD, Madison, WI). Non-hydrogen atoms were refined with anisotropic displacement coefficients, and hydrogen atoms were treated as idealized contributions. SADABS (Sheldrick, 12 G.M. Crystallographic data has been deposited with the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Center and is available free of charge through the CCDC online database.

### Electrochemistry

Cyclic voltammetry experiments were conducted under N2 or Ar at 295 ± 3 K using a standard three-electrode setup consisting of a PEEK-encased glassy carbon working electrode (ϕ = 1 mm) and Type 2 graphite rod counter electrode (ϕ = 3 mm). The Ag/AgCl pseudoreference electrode was stored in a glass compartment containing solvent and electrolyte and was separated from the bulk solution using a porous glass frit (Coralpor). The working electrode was polished with 0.25 μm diamond polishing paste and lapping oil in the glovebox and thoroughly rinsed with the solvent used in the corresponding experiment. A Gamry Reference 1010B potentiostat and Gamry software were used for data collection/analysis. Samples typically contained 0.1 M [nBu4N]­[B­(C6F5)4], organic solvent (3 mL), and 1.0 mM analyte. All CVs are referenced internally to the Cp2Fe+/0 redox couple (0 V).
